worst_places.quote: The ENTRYPOINT will execute sh -c python app.py arg1 arg2 as a shell command
worst_places.problem: docker-quiz-2 marks this as the correct answer (correctIndex 2), but it is wrong, and the file contradicts itself two items later. Run arguments REPLACE CMD, they are not appended to it: `docker run myimage arg1 arg2` against `ENTRYPOINT ["sh","-c"]` + `CMD ["python","app.py"]` runs `sh -c arg1 arg2`, not `sh -c python app.py arg1 arg2`. The item's own explanation states the correct rule while the marked option breaks it ("CMD provides default arguments that can be overridden by command-line arguments passed to docker run"), and docker-quiz-10 and docker-quiz-13 both state the correct rule outright ("the arg overrides CMD but not ENTRYPOINT" / "they override CMD but are appended to ENTRYPOINT"). cicd-devops/04-docker-essentials.md says the same: "docker run my-app:1.0 /bin/sh   # CMD replaced". A reader who has learned the rule correctly is told they are wrong by the only Docker quiz on the site.
worst_places.before: Options: [0] The ENTRYPOINT will execute sh -c, and CMD will be ignored because ENTRYPOINT is defined / [1] The CMD will execute and the arguments arg1 arg2 will be passed to python app.py / [2] The ENTRYPOINT will execute sh -c python app.py arg1 arg2 as a shell command (marked correct) / [3] An error will occur because both CMD and ENTRYPOINT cannot be defined together
worst_places.after: Options: [0] It runs sh -c arg1 arg2 — the run arguments replace CMD, so python app.py is never used (mark this correct) / [1] It runs sh -c python app.py arg1 arg2 — CMD is kept and the run arguments are added after it / [2] It runs python app.py and ignores both arg1 and arg2 / [3] It fails, because CMD and ENTRYPOINT cannot both be set. Explanation: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable. CMD is only the default argument list. Any arguments you pass to docker run replace CMD completely — they are not added to it. So `docker run myimage arg1 arg2` runs `sh -c arg1 arg2`: sh treats arg1 as the command and arg2 as $0. To keep python app.py you have to leave the run arguments out.

Line by line:
- `FROM` picks the base image. An Alpine-based Node image is common because it is small.
- `WORKDIR` sets the directory the following instructions run in. It creates that directory if it does not exist.
- `COPY` brings files from the build context into the image.
- `RUN` executes a command at build time and saves the result as a layer.
- `EXPOSE` is documentation only. It tells readers and tools like `docker inspect` which port the app expects. It publishes nothing.
- `CMD` sets the default command a container runs when it starts from this image. You can override it at `docker run` time.

worst_places.before: A container instead runs directly on the host OS kernel: it uses Linux namespaces (PID, network, mount, and others) to get its own isolated view of processes, network, and filesystem, and cgroups to limit CPU/memory usage.
worst_places.after: A container runs directly on the host machine's own kernel — the core of the operating system that manages processes, memory and hardware. It gets its isolation from two Linux kernel features. **Namespaces** give the container its own private view of the machine: its own process list (the PID namespace, where PID is a process id), its own network stack, its own filesystem mounts. **cgroups** (control groups) cap how much CPU time and memory it may use.

There is no single trick here. Four independent techniques stack up:

**1. Multi-stage builds.** Copy only the pruned production dependencies and the built artifacts into a separate runtime stage. Build tooling and the full `node_modules` tree, devDependencies included, never reach the final image.

**2. A minimal base image.** An `-alpine` variant cuts the base OS (operating system) files down sharply. A distroless image such as `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs18-debian11` goes further still: no shell, no package manager, no OS utilities — just a runtime and your app. That also shrinks the attack surface, because there is less inside for an attacker to use.

worst_places.before: `--memory` (or `mem_limit`/`deploy.resources.limits.memory` in Compose) caps how much RAM a container can use; if it tries to exceed that, the kernel's OOM killer terminates the container's main process rather than letting it slowly degrade the whole host.
worst_places.after: `--memory` caps how much memory (RAM) the container may use. In Compose the same cap is `mem_limit`, or `deploy.resources.limits.memory`. If the container tries to go over that cap, the kernel's OOM killer (out-of-memory killer) terminates the container's main process outright. That is deliberate: a hard kill is better than one container slowly dragging down the whole host.

worst_places.after: A named volume is created and tracked by Docker itself. It lives in Docker's own storage area — `/var/lib/docker/volumes/...` on Linux. Its lifecycle does not depend on any single container: you refer to it by name and Docker decides where it physically sits. Two things follow from that. It is portable across hosts that use the same driver. And it is easy to back up: start a throwaway container, mount the volume into it, copy the data out.

The quiz layer is not a language problem, it is an unedited generated artefact. Five signals, all mechanical and all invisible to a prose-level flag script: (1) zero ``` fences in the entire file, so all five code snippets render as stray language tags plus unformatted text; (2) ids jump 1-5, 7, 9-10, 12-15 — three items were deleted from a generated set of 15 and nothing was renumbered or re-balanced; (3) two snippets are decoration that contradicts their own answer (quiz-14's `VOLUME` declares the anonymous volume the answer warns against) or cannot build (quiz-12); (4) three stems glue two or three questions together and only the last one matches the options; (5) 12 items cover just 6 concepts — CMD-vs-ENTRYPOINT three times (quiz-2, -10, -13), volumes three times (quiz-5, -9, -14), multi-stage twice (quiz-4, -12) — while 14 of the bank's 20 topics (limits, health checks, non-root USER, BuildKit cache, .dockerignore, signals, socket) are never assessed at all.
